contrastMetadata.transferBoundary: Endpoint-only state supports a pair or read/write relation; aggregate, frequency, or membership state representing every element in a changing interval supports a window, even when only two index variables are visible.

authoringProvenance.author: OpenAI GPT-5.6 Pro — candidate authoring; human review required

items.prompt: Which state description is the decisive signal for a sliding window rather than an endpoint-pair two-pointers scan?

options.text: State such as a sum or frequency map that summarizes the current contiguous [left, right] and is updated as elements enter or leave.
Only the current endpoint values and their relation.
Two integer indices named left and right.
A loop that visits each position at most a few times.

feedback.reason: A window owns state for the complete contiguous candidate, not just its endpoints.

blocks.text: Sliding window gains efficiency by updating a summary of the current range when one element enters or leaves. The summary may be a sum, count, frequency map, deque, or another structure, but its semantics cover every member of [left, right]. Pair-oriented two pointers may use only endpoint values or role-specific state such as read and write positions. Both can be linear and use two indices, so those surface properties are not decisive. The state ownership test transfers across implementations even when data structures differ.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.endpoint_values: Endpoint-only state is consistent with pair-oriented two pointers, not evidence that the whole range is maintained.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.two_indices: Both families and many unrelated algorithms can use two indices; the count does not reveal whether they select a pair, define roles, or bound range-owned state.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.linear_loop: Both pair scans and windows can be amortized linear; runtime shape does not reveal whether the candidate is an endpoint relation or a maintained contiguous range.

constraints: Classify the algorithm by what its maintained state denotes, not by variable names or asymptotic complexity.

items.prompt: To compute every length-k moving average, an algorithm adds the new right value and subtracts the value that just left at right - k. The width never varies. Which classification is correct?

options.text: A fixed-size sliding window.
Two pointers, because the distance between boundaries is fixed.
Neither family, because a window must change size.

feedback.reason: The maintained sum belongs to a contiguous interval that moves, even though its size is constant.

blocks.text: “Sliding” refers to the candidate range moving through the sequence, not necessarily to variable width. The algorithm reuses the previous range sum by adding the entrant and removing the leaver, so the state continuously represents exactly k contiguous elements. A two-pointers classification based on fixed distance would miss this aggregate ownership. Variable-window shrink rules are unnecessary here because the size condition itself determines which element leaves.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.fixed_two_pointer_state: A fixed gap does not override the fact that the sum represents every member of the moving interval.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.neither_width_constant: Fixed-size windows are canonical sliding windows; variable width is only one variant.

constraints: 1 <= k <= the sequence length.
The output is required for every contiguous block of length k.

items.prompt: A variable-length window over nonnegative numbers stores only one scalar, currentSum, plus left and right. Does O(1) auxiliary state make it an endpoint-only two-pointers algorithm?

options.text: No. currentSum semantically represents all elements in the current range.
Yes. Window state must grow with the window.
Yes. Sliding window requires a frequency map.
It depends on whether the variables are named start and end.

feedback.reason: State semantics, not memory size, determine whether the full interval is maintained.

blocks.text: A scalar sum is compressed range state: changing any member of the window can change the value, and adding or removing a boundary member updates it. Sliding windows do not require storage proportional to their width, nor do they require a map. Conversely, a two-pointers algorithm can carry substantial auxiliary state while still reasoning about endpoint or read/write relations. The robust question is what the state denotes, not how many machine words it occupies.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.yes_constant_state: A range summary can be constant-size; storage growth is not a defining requirement.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.yes_no_frequency_map: A frequency map is only one representation; sums, counts, deques, or fixed scalars can still summarize every member of the current range.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.depends_on_names: Names such as left and right are arbitrary; the invariant is determined by what currentSum denotes and how entering and leaving elements update it.

constraints: currentSum is always equal to the sum of elements in the current inclusive range.

items.prompt: During in-place deduplication of a sorted array, read scans candidates and write marks the last accepted output position. No summary is maintained for the elements between them. Which state model applies?

options.text: Fixed role state for two pointers: read explores and write marks the compacted prefix.
Variable window state for every element between read and write.
Both, because the indices enclose a contiguous region.

feedback.reason: The indices encode distinct roles, while the enclosed region is not one maintained candidate.

blocks.text: The algorithm's invariant concerns the compacted output prefix and the next input candidate. The gap may contain processed or rejected values, but their collective membership is not summarized or validated. That makes the state endpoint- and role-oriented rather than window-oriented. A contiguous geometric region exists, yet it is not the semantic object being optimized or kept valid. This distinction is especially useful for same-direction code, where pointer direction offers little diagnostic help.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.window_membership: The algorithm does not maintain or validate all elements in the gap as one candidate.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.both_equivalent: Geometric enclosure is insufficient; the state and invariant assign different semantics.

constraints: The accepted output prefix remains sorted and duplicate-free.
No aggregate describes the read/write gap.

items.prompt: A problem originally asks for a pair of sorted values with a target difference. It is changed so that values may appear in arbitrary order and the answer must be the longest original-order contiguous segment in which no value appears more than twice. What state change is required?

options.text: Maintain per-value frequencies for every element in the current segment, using a sliding-window state.
Keep only the two endpoint values; interior multiplicities are irrelevant.
Use the original pair state because the implementation still has left and right.
Sort the segment after every right step and keep pair state.

feedback.reason: Interior multiplicities become part of validity, so endpoint-only state is no longer sufficient.

blocks.text: Because the revised input is not sorted, equal values may occur anywhere inside the current segment. The condition can therefore change when any interior member enters or leaves, not merely when endpoint values are compared. A frequency structure representing the current contiguous segment is material state: increment the entering value, decrement the leaving value, and shrink until every count is at most two. Reusing the old pair state would omit exactly the information the new constraint asks about. The transfer rule is to expand state ownership when the answer contract begins to depend on every range member.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.endpoint_only: Endpoint values cannot determine whether an interior value occurs three times.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.same_pair_state: Shared index names do not preserve a state contract after the validity condition changes.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_again: Sorting a candidate changes its original-order adjacency, so it no longer represents the required contiguous segment; repeating that work also misses the reusable range-state invariant.

constraints: The revised input may contain equal values at nonadjacent positions.
The revised answer must be a contiguous segment in original order.

items.prompt: A task asks for the sum of every contiguous block of exactly m elements. Which state model is the direct fit?

options.text: A fixed-size window with one aggregate updated when the next element enters and the oldest leaves.
Endpoint-only pair state, because only left and right indices are visible.
A variable window that shrinks whenever the sum exceeds a threshold, even though length must equal m.
Sort values before each block so endpoints summarize the block sum.

feedback.reason: The candidate is a contiguous range with invariant length, and every interior value contributes to its sum.

blocks.text: A fixed-size window advances one position at a time: add the entering value and subtract the leaving value. No validity-driven shrink is needed because the size contract is exact. Endpoint-only state would lose interior contributions, and sorting would change which original positions form each requested block. The two indices are boundaries of a range-owned aggregate.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.endpoint_pair: The sum depends on all m values, not only on the two endpoint values.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.variable_shrink: The contract fixes length exactly; shrinking on a sum predicate would produce the wrong candidate sizes.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_values: Blocks are defined by original contiguity, so reordering values changes the problem.

constraints: m is fixed and every value in the original-order block contributes.

items.prompt: A variable-length window tracks the longest nonnegative-sum segment whose total is at most B. Which state change distinguishes it from a fixed-size scan?

options.text: The left boundary moves by a predicate on the aggregate, so window length changes to restore validity after right expands.
The length is always m, so left moves exactly once per right step.
Only the values at left and right are compared; interior sum is not part of state.
Sorting is required before any left-boundary movement.

feedback.reason: Variable windows are governed by validity and can shrink multiple positions, whereas fixed windows are governed by a prescribed size.

blocks.text: After adding a nonnegative value on the right, the total can exceed B. Removing values from the left cannot increase the sum, so repeated eviction restores the predicate and leaves the longest valid suffix for that right endpoint. The size is an output of the validity process rather than a constant. Endpoint comparison or sorting would omit the range-owned sum invariant.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.fixed_length_only: The length changes with the budget predicate and may shrink by more than one position.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.endpoint_compare: The full range sum determines validity, so interior values are material.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_before_shrink: Original-order contiguity and nonnegative monotonicity, not value sorting, justify the shrink rule.

constraints: All values are nonnegative and the result preserves original order.

items.prompt: Two algorithms use left and right indices. Algorithm A compares only a[left] and a[right] in a sorted array. Algorithm B maintains counts for every value from left through right. What does the state difference imply?

options.text: A has endpoint-only two-pointer state; B has range-owned sliding-window state, even though the loop variables look identical.
They are the same pattern because both increment left or right.
Both are windows because both intervals have two boundaries.
Both are pairs because a window's endpoints are the only selected positions.

feedback.reason: The maintained state reveals whether interior elements are semantically part of the candidate.

blocks.text: Algorithm A can justify movement from sorted endpoint relations and does not need to update state for the interior. Algorithm B must increment and decrement counts as boundaries move, because every range member affects validity. Identical variable names and movement syntax do not erase that proof distinction; state ownership is the stronger signal.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.same_by_names: Names and pointer operations are shared representations, not a shared invariant.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.both_windows: A's interior is not a maintained candidate, so it lacks window semantics.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.both_pairs: B's frequency state proves that interior values affect its answer.

constraints: Algorithm B's count map exactly matches the current interval.

items.prompt: Select all conditions that justify treating [left, right] as a sliding-window state rather than endpoint-only state.

options.text: The sum of every element in the interval affects validity or score.
A frequency map is updated when elements enter and leave the interval.
Only the two endpoint values are compared in a sorted array.
One index marks the next output position while another scans input.

feedback.reason: Range-owned aggregate or membership state makes interior elements part of the candidate and requires boundary updates.

blocks.text: A full-range sum or frequency map must be updated when right expands and left evicts, which is the operational signature of a window. Endpoint relations and read/write compaction use different state: one compares selected positions, the other builds a retained prefix. Two indices alone cannot distinguish these cases.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.endpoint_relation: Endpoint-only state is evidence for a pair relation, not a range-owned window.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.read_write_roles: Read/write indices have distinct compaction roles and do not describe a live aggregate over the interval.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.full_range_sum: Interior contributions make the interval the complete candidate.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.frequency_map: Boundary updates maintain state for every current range member.

constraints: More than one condition is correct.

items.prompt: A fixed-size window and a variable-size window can use the same left/right variables. What should a reviewer compare first?

options.text: Whether left moves on a fixed schedule to preserve size or moves in response to a validity predicate and its state repair.
Whether the variables are named left and right in both implementations.
Whether the values are sorted, because every window requires sorted input.
Whether both loops run in O(n), because equal complexity makes them identical.

feedback.reason: The window subtype is defined by how the boundaries are constrained and repaired, not by names or asymptotic complexity.

blocks.text: In a fixed window, right advances and left follows to preserve a declared length. In a variable window, right may create an invalid state and left advances zero or more times until the predicate holds. Both can be O(n) and both can run on unsorted input. The boundary-update contract tells the reviewer which state invariant the code must preserve.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.variable_names: Names do not show whether the range length or validity predicate controls movement.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_order: Window state is usually defined over original order and does not require sorted values.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.loop_count: Equal O(n) bounds do not make fixed-size and validity-driven updates the same algorithm.

constraints: The reviewer is given only loop structure and must recover the update contract.

items.prompt: What does a fixed-size window's left pointer usually do after the first k elements are loaded?
constraints: The contrast boundary must be identified from state semantics.
The output contract is fixed for this item.

options.text: Advance one position for each right shift so the range always contains exactly k elements.
Move only when a predicate fails.
Move based on comparing the two endpoint values.
Return to zero after each output.

feedback.reason: The accepted option uses the contrasted state invariant rather than surface syntax.

blocks.text: Two variables, a loop, or linear complexity can appear in both patterns. The decisive evidence is what the retained state represents and which pointer movement the proof permits.

The variables are called left and right.
The input is sorted.
The loop is O(n).

feedback.reason: The accepted option uses the contrasted state invariant rather than surface syntax.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sorted: Windows can operate on original unsorted order.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.linear: Both fixed and variable windows can be linear.

constraints: The contrast boundary must be identified from state semantics.

options.text: Variable-size window: validity controls how far left moves after expansion.
Fixed-size window because both endpoints exist.
Two-pointer pair search because only two indices are named.
Binary search because a condition changes.

Use the whole input as a substitute.

Shrink k until a window exists.
